ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows an arrow-pushing mechanism. The upper fragment is in an enolate/enoxy anion form: the upper oxygen atom carries a negative charge and forms a single bond with the adjacent carbon; there is a C=C double bond between this carbon and the alkene carbon on the left, and substituents such as R, R1 are labeled nearby. There is also a carbonyl fragment below; the carbonyl carbon is connected to R2, R3 substituents, and the oxygen is below. The curved arrows show three steps of electron movement: the electrons of the upper O⁻ push back to form the upper C=O; the π electrons of the adjacent C=C move downward to form a new C–C σ bond with the lower carbonyl carbon; the π electrons of the lower C=O move to the oxygen to form O⁻. Reasoning: After rearrangement according to the arrows, the upper part becomes a carbonyl; the original alkene becomes a single bond and connects with the lower carbonyl carbon; the lower carbonyl becomes an alkoxide anion. Preserve the original R/R1/R2/R3 substituents and represent them with the wildcard [*], obtaining a beta-alkoxide carbonyl skeleton, corresponding to the SMILES O=C(CC([*])([O-])[*])[*].

method.method_draft: First describe the drawn substrate and arrows. Keep all R/R1/R2/R3 groups attached to their original atoms. Then write the resulting beta-alkoxide carbonyl skeleton with wildcard substituents as the SMILES `O=C(CC([*])([O-])[*])[*]`.

method.method_draft: Create a graph from the drawing, labeling only the reactive atoms and treating each R group as a wildcard substituent. Apply the three graph edits indicated by the arrows: set Oa=Ca, set Ca–Cb single, add Cb–Cc single, set Cc–Ob single and assign Ob as `[O-]`. After these edits, traverse the product graph from the newly formed upper carbonyl: carbonyl carbon attached to one wildcard substituent and to a two-carbon chain ending at a tetrahedral carbon bearing `[O-]` and two wildcard substituents. Encode that graph as `O=C(CC([*])([O-])[*])[*]`.
